back: One party in a transaction has more or better information than the other. In credit markets, the borrower knows more about their financial state, repayment ability, and risk than the lender.
Pre-contract / ex-ante information problem. Lenders cannot distinguish high-risk from low-risk borrowers; with pooled pricing, low-risk borrowers exit and the pool worsens. Akerlof's lemons.
Post-contract / ex-post information problem. Once funded or insured, a party takes more risk because they don't bear the full downside. Borrower harms lender, not the other way around.
Banks restrict the QUANTITY of credit rather than raise the price. Higher rates would worsen the borrower pool (adverse selection) and incentivise risky projects (moral hazard). Stiglitz–Weiss.
Ex-ante effort to identify borrower quality before lending. Credit-scoring, financial-statement analysis, risk-based pricing. Mitigates adverse selection.
Ex-post effort to observe borrower behaviour after lending. Covenants, regular reporting, site visits, performance reviews. Mitigates moral hazard.

Affirmative (must do — provide statements, maintain insurance), Negative (must not do — extra debt, dividends, asset sales), Financial (ratios — debt/equity, ICR), Reporting (deliver data), Operational (restrict activities).
(1) Adverse selection: risky borrowers less willing to pledge collateral → self-selection signal. (2) Moral hazard: borrower has skin in the game → less risk-shifting after disbursal.

When a covenant is breached, the bank can grant a waiver — choosing not to enforce its remedies. Reasons: maintain relationship, breach is minor/temporary, borrower viable, enforcement would worsen losses, prelude to renegotiation.
Asymmetric information about quality leads to market unravelling. Buyers price-down, high-quality sellers exit, only lemons remain. Foundational adverse-selection model.
Bank's expected return is non-monotonic in loan rate r. Beyond r*, raising rates worsens pool quality and incentives more than the price gain. Banks ration credit at r* rather than clear the market.
Long-run lending relationships reveal private borrower information over time, reducing asymmetric information. Banks gain a soft-information advantage and can lend at better terms.
Banks act as agents for many savers, monitoring borrowers on their behalf. Economies of scale + diversification make it cheaper than each saver monitoring directly. Justifies the bank intermediary.
Banks transform claim attributes along five dimensions: duration, divisibility, liquidity, credit risk, currency. Source of both value and fragility.

1. Duration (long mortgages from short deposits). 2. Divisibility (large loans from small deposits). 3. Liquidity (illiquid assets, liquid liabilities). 4. Credit risk (risky assets, safe deposits). 5. Numeraire (foreign assets, domestic liabilities).
Banks fund long-term assets with short-term liabilities, earning a margin from the upward-sloping yield curve. Creates liquidity, funding, and interest-rate risk.
Banks hold only a fraction of deposits as reserves and lend out the remainder. Relies on most depositors not withdrawing simultaneously. Multiplies money supply via the deposit multiplier.
Inside money = bank-created (deposits, loans). Outside money = central bank money (banknotes, reserves). Modern money is mostly inside money — created when banks lend.
Bank funds short (money market) and invests long (fixed-rate bonds). Earns positive carry on upward-sloping curve; loses on inversion. Risks: interest-rate risk, funding risk, yield-curve inversion.
NIM = NII / Average Assets. Headline measure of how efficiently a bank earns spread between asset yield and funding cost. Typical bank NIM: 1–3%.

Deposits / Loans. Below 100% means the bank funds part of its lending with non-deposit sources (wholesale funding, debt securities, equity). Lower ratio = greater wholesale funding reliance = higher liquidity risk.
Gross loans = exposure before impairment. Net loans = gross − accumulated impairment. The balance sheet shows net; gross requires adding back the impairment provision.

front: Bank balance sheet — assets vs liabilities (typical)
back: Assets (use of funds): loans, securities, cash & central-bank reserves, interbank claims. Liabilities (sources): deposits, wholesale funding, subordinated debt, equity. The fundamental mismatch creates QAT risks.
ROE = ROA × (Assets/Equity). Banks operate with ~5–10% equity (10–20× leverage). A 1% ROA + 15× leverage = 15% ROE. Leverage amplifies returns but also losses → why capital regulation matters.
Distinguished by MATURITY, not liquidity. Money markets: <12-month instruments (T-bills, CP, repo, interbank). Capital markets: >12-month (bonds, equity).
Likelihood that a borrower defaults within a horizon (typically 1 year). Estimated from internal models or external ratings. Drives expected and unexpected loss.
Percentage of exposure not recovered after default = 1 − Recovery Rate. Depends on collateral, seniority, jurisdiction. Multiplies into Expected Loss.
The amount owed at the moment of default — includes accrued interest, drawn balances, expected drawdown of undrawn commitments. Typically larger than current balance for credit lines.
EL = PD × LGD × EAD. Covered by impairment PROVISIONS — accounting expense, not capital.
Tail risk at 99.9% confidence over 1-year horizon. Covered by regulatory CAPITAL, not provisions. The job of capital is to absorb losses BEYOND the expected.
Stage 1: performing (12-month ECL). Stage 2: significant increase in credit risk since origination (lifetime ECL). Stage 3: credit-impaired / default (lifetime ECL with PD = 100%).
12-month ECL = EAD × PD₁₂ₘ × LGD. Applied to all performing loans at origination and as long as no significant increase in credit risk has occurred.
Lifetime ECL = EAD × PD_lifetime × LGD. Triggered by significant increase in credit risk (SICR). Provisioning becomes much heavier than Stage 1.
Default has occurred; PD = 100%. Impairment = EAD × LGD. Interest income calculated on net (post-impairment) carrying amount, not gross.

front: SICR — Significant Increase in Credit Risk
back: Trigger for Stage 1 → Stage 2 migration. Measured by changes in PD since origination, NOT by collateral value alone. Lower collateral matters only if it signals higher PD.

front: Why lifetime PD declines over time
back: Lifetime PD measures default risk over remaining life of the loan. As time passes and the loan amortises, less time remains during which default can occur — so lifetime PD mechanically falls, even with constant credit quality.
Notional amount of an asset multiplied by its risk weight. Capital ratios are computed against RWA, not raw assets. Different approaches: standardised (regulator-set weights), IRB (bank-estimated).
EU equivalent term for RWA. Total REA = Credit REA + Market REA + Operational REA. Capital ratios are over Total REA.
Regulator-prescribed risk weights based on external ratings. Sovereigns 0%, retail mortgages 35%, corporates 100% (unrated). Simple and transparent but blunt.
Bank estimates own PD; regulator supplies LGD and EAD. More risk-sensitive than standardised but less than IRB Advanced. Requires regulatory approval.
Bank estimates ALL parameters (PD, LGD, EAD, M). Most risk-sensitive but most demanding in terms of data, models, governance, and regulatory scrutiny. Norwegian banks heavily use IRB.
Acc. impairment Y2 = Acc. impairment Y1 + new impairments charged − write-offs. Solve for the unknown. Common exam question (Mid-term 2024 P1Q5).
Highest-quality regulatory capital. Common equity less deductions (goodwill, proposed dividends, intangibles). Minimum 4.5% of RWA under Basel III.
Hybrid / contingent convertible capital. Perpetual; can be converted to equity or written down on going-concern basis. Coupon at bank's discretion. Minimum 1.5% (or fill with CET1).
Subordinated debt. Only written down in resolution or liquidation (gone-concern). Minimum 2% (or fill with CET1/AT1). Total Pillar 1 minimum: 8%.
Universal minimum capital requirement: 8% Total / 6% T1 / 4.5% CET1 of RWA. Same for all banks. Designed to cover unexpected loss.
Bank-specific minimum on top of Pillar 1, set by the supervisor based on the bank's risk profile (interest-rate risk, concentration risk, etc.). Mandatory.
Bank-specific guidance for additional capital that the bank should hold under stress, but breach does not automatically restrict distributions. Soft requirement.
+2.5% CET1 above Pillar 1 minimum. Designed to be drawn down in stress. Breach restricts dividend/AT1/bonus payments via the Maximum Distributable Amount (MDA).
0–2.5% CET1, set by national authorities based on credit cycle. Built up in booms, released in busts. In Norway: currently 2.5%.
CET1 buffer to address structural systemic risk in a country or sector. In Norway: 4.5%. Combined with G-SIB/O-SII buffers for individual systemic banks.
CET1 buffer for Other Systemically Important Institutions (national systemically important banks). DNB and Sparebank 1 in Norway carry 2.0%.
Tier 1 / Total Exposures (unweighted). Basel III minimum 3%. Non-risk-sensitive backstop against RWA gaming or model failure.
HQLA / Net cash outflow over 30 days ≥ 100%. Ensures the bank can survive a 30-day stress run on its own liquidity.
Available Stable Funding / Required Stable Funding (1-year) ≥ 100%. Ensures sustainable funding structure beyond the 30-day LCR window.

front: MREL — Minimum Requirement for Own Funds and Eligible Liabilities
back: (Own Funds + Eligible Liabilities) / RWA. Bank-specific. Ensures enough bail-in-able liabilities exist BEFORE a crisis. Two parts: Loss Absorption Amount + Recapitalisation Amount.
FSB standard for global systemically important banks (G-SIBs). Minimum 16–18% of RWA. EU equivalent integrated with MREL.
Simple 8% capital ratio with crude risk weights (sovereigns 0%, banks 20%, mortgages 50%, corporates 100%). Credited with stabilising the 1990s but criticised for risk insensitivity.
Three pillars: (1) minimum capital with IRB models, (2) supervisory review, (3) market discipline. Added operational risk. Procyclical risk weights criticised after the 2008 crisis.
Post-2008 overhaul: stricter CET1, capital buffers, leverage ratio, LCR + NSFR, MREL. Implemented in EU through CRR/CRD IV; CRR3/CRD VI is the latest update.
~18%: 4.5% min + 1.7% P2R + 2.5% conservation + 2.5% countercyclical + 4.5% systemic + 2.0% O-SII + 1.0% P2G. Total capital requirement ~22%.
1. Risk-sensitive: capital adequacy ratio = Own Funds / RWA. 2. Non-risk-sensitive: leverage ratio = Tier 1 / Total Exposures. 3. Bail-in capital: MREL = (Own Funds + Eligible Liabilities) / RWA.
Pooling loans into a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) and issuing tranches of bonds backed by the pool. Originate-to-distribute model. Transfers credit risk and (in true-sale form) provides funding.
Off-balance-sheet entity that holds the loan pool in a true-sale securitisation. Bankruptcy-remote from the originating bank. Issues tranches to fund the pool.
Cash flows from the pool are paid in waterfall sequence: senior (AAA, lowest yield) → mezzanine → equity (first loss, highest yield). Senior is protected by subordination.
Junior tranches absorb losses first, protecting senior tranches. The most common form of credit enhancement. Combined with overcollateralisation, reserve accounts, excess spread.
Securitisation pooling already-securitised assets (typically MBS tranches) and re-tranching them. Created supposedly safe AAA from BBB MBS — until correlation broke in 2008.
CDO of CDOs. Pool of mezzanine tranches from multiple CDOs, re-tranched into a new senior/mezzanine/equity structure. Extreme opacity; senior tranches defaulted en masse in 2008.
Loans STAY on balance sheet; credit risk is transferred via CDS or guarantees on a reference pool. Provides CAPITAL RELIEF but NO funding. CDS plays the central role.
Loans are legally SOLD to the SPV. Both funding and capital relief. Loans leave the originating bank's balance sheet entirely.
Securitised pool of mortgages. Agency MBS (Fannie/Freddie/Ginnie) carry US government guarantees; private-label (non-agency) MBS pools subprime/Alt-A and have no guarantee.
Bank originates loans then immediately sells them to investors or SPVs. Removes credit risk and funding need. BUT weakens screening incentive — central GFC failure mode.
Issuer-pays conflict of interest; models calibrated on benign housing-price periods; correlation underestimated; rapid downgrades when crisis broke. AAA tranches defaulted.

Bilateral derivative: protection buyer pays a periodic spread; seller pays out on a credit event (default, restructuring). Used to hedge credit risk OR to take views OR to construct synthetic securitisations.

AIG Financial Products had sold CDS protection on ~$440bn of structured-credit reference assets. Collateral calls mounted as ratings fell; AIG became insolvent. Fed bailed out at $85bn for 79.9% equity (Sep 2008).

Off-balance-sheet vehicle that funds longer-term ABS holdings with short-term Asset-Backed Commercial Paper. When ABCP markets froze (Aug 2007), conduits could not roll funding; sponsors were forced to absorb them back.
Off-balance-sheet entity funding long-dated ABS/CDOs with short-term ABCP and medium-term notes. Maturity mismatch monetised the yield spread — until ABCP markets froze.

Simultaneous spot exchange of two currencies + agreement to reverse the exchange at a forward rate F at a future date. Economically a collateralised loan: one currency pledged to borrow the other. No interim interest payments.
F = S₀ × (1 + r_quote × t) / (1 + r_base × t). Forward premium/discount equals the interest differential. No-arbitrage condition. Deviations = cross-currency basis.
F − S₀ = forward minus spot. Compensation embedded in the exchange rate for the interest-rate differential. Positive when quote currency has higher rate. Quoted in pips.
S₀ = 1.65, r_NOK = 4%, r_DKK = 2%, t = 0.5. F = 1.65 × 1.02/1.01 = 1.67. Swap points = 0.02 = 2 points (200 pips). NOK has higher rate, so DKK forward is at a premium.

Long-dated (1–30y) instrument: principal exchange at SPOT + periodic floating-rate payments in each currency + final re-exchange at SAME spot. Interest differential delivered through coupon legs, not forward rate.
Deviation from CIP. Added to one leg of the CCBS (typically non-USD) to reflect counterparty risk, supply/demand, and capital constraints. Widened sharply in 2008 (USD scarce) and 2020.
Same-currency swap: one party pays fixed, receives floating; the other does the reverse. No principal exchange. TRANSFORMS interest-rate risk (price risk → cash-flow risk) — does not eliminate it.

front: IRS transforms but does not eliminate risk
back: Fixed → floating removes price risk (mark-to-market sensitivity) but introduces cash-flow risk (variable interest payments). Floating → fixed locks in cash flows but means MTM losses when rates fall.
Issue EUR fixed bond → enter EUR IRS (receive fixed, pay EURIBOR) → enter EUR/NOK CCBS (receive EURIBOR, pay NIBOR − basis). Net: NIBOR + spread − basis. Clean floating NOK exposure.
Foreign equity values fell → Norwegian investors over-hedged → must buy more foreign currency to honour hedge → must sell NOK → adds to NOK selling pressure → NOK depreciates further.
NOK depreciated → mark-to-market losses on FX hedges → margin calls → NBFIs sold Norwegian bonds to raise cash → bond prices fell, risk premiums spiked. Bond fire sales.
13 March: extra liquidity + 50bp rate cut. 18 March: collateral framework changes. 19 March: press release on possible FX intervention. 20 March: 75bp rate cut to 0.25%. 7 May: rate to zero.

Standing facility: Fed lends USD to foreign central banks against their currency. Activated unlimited in October 2008 and March 2020 — collapsed the negative dollar basis within weeks. Critical international LOLR tool.

front: Derivatives create liquidity risk (despite hedging price risk)
back: Derivatives reduce price risk but create LIQUIDITY risk via margin/collateral requirements. Adverse MTM moves trigger immediate cash demands — SVB and March 2020 are textbook cases.

Self-fulfilling panic where depositors withdraw because they expect others to withdraw. Converts illiquidity into insolvency through forced asset sales. Resolved via deposit insurance, LOLR, or suspension of convertibility.
Illiquid: assets > liabilities at fair value, but cannot meet short-term obligations. Insolvent: liabilities > assets. LOLR can solve illiquidity; only recapitalisation solves insolvency.
Central bank role: lend freely, at penalty rate, against good collateral, to solvent-but-illiquid banks. Bagehot's Rule (1873). Distinguishes liquidity support from solvency bailout.
In a panic, the central bank should lend freely, at a penalty rate, against good collateral. Foundational principle of LOLR. Distinguishes legitimate liquidity support from bailout.

1. Macro-imbalances (savings glut, low rates). 2. Financial innovation + shadow banking. 3. Misplaced reliance on math/models. 4. Procyclicality (haircuts, margins, ratings). 5. Lack of confidence/transparency. 6. Trigger: US subprime.

SIVs, ABCP conduits, money-market funds, investment banks (30–50× leverage) — maturity transformation OUTSIDE the regulated banking system. No deposit insurance, no LOLR access. Repo runs and ABCP freezes.
Falling ratings → wider haircuts/margins → forced selling → falling prices → further rating downgrades. Mark-to-market accounting + VaR risk-management amplified the cycle.
9 Aug 2007: BNP suspended redemptions on three ABS funds, citing inability to value assets. Froze European ABCP market overnight. ECB injected €95bn same day. Marked the start of the GFC.
UK mortgage lender with ~75% wholesale funding. First UK bank run since 1866 (Overend & Gurney). Visible queues outside branches AFTER BoE LOLR support became public. Nationalised Feb 2008.
Run on repo funding; counterparties refused to roll overnight. Fed provided $29bn emergency facility (Section 13(3)); JPMorgan acquired at $10/share. First major investment-bank failure of GFC.

$613bn Chapter 11 bankruptcy — largest in US history. Triggered global money-market panic; Reserve Primary Fund broke the buck. Decision NOT to rescue Lehman is widely seen as the worst policy mistake of the crisis.
$85bn Fed revolving credit facility for 79.9% equity stake. AIG's CDS book on structured credit was insolvent. Bailout prevented cascade of CDS losses across global banks.

Long-duration HTM bond losses (~$15.9bn unrealised) + concentrated uninsured deposits → social-media-driven run. Capital ratios LOOKED fine; economic reality was different. FDIC invoked Systemic Risk Exception.
Forced merger with UBS by Swiss authorities + CHF 100bn liquidity + CHF 9bn loss guarantee. AT1 written down BEFORE equity — controversial hierarchy breach. Repriced AT1 markets globally.

Norway/Sweden/Finland: post-deregulation credit boom + asset bubble + maturity mismatch. Norway: state ownership of three big banks. Sweden: blanket guarantee + bad banks. Finland: severe (13% of GDP losses).
Deregulation + flat-rate deposit insurance + interest-rate spike → S&Ls insolvent on cost basis but kept open via forbearance → eventual large losses. ~1000 institutions failed; $124bn taxpayer cost.
Government guarantee on deposits up to a limit. Solves Diamond–Dybvig coordination problem by removing incentive to run. Coverage: EU/EEA €100k; Norway NOK 2m per depositor per bank.
Deposit-insurance scheme guaranteeing deposits up to NOK 2 million per customer per bank. Funded by ex-ante contributions from member banks. Higher coverage than EU minimum.

Deposit insurance CREATES moral hazard — banks can take more risk without paying higher funding cost (depositors don't care). Mitigants: risk-based premiums, capital requirements, prudential supervision.

Deposit insurance is a put option held by the bank's shareholders. Value rises with asset volatility (σ) and leverage (D/A). Flat-rate insurance underprices risk for risky banks → moral hazard. Risk-based premiums needed.

front: If super-preference removed from deposit insurance fund
back: Fund faces higher loss risk → reduced ability to finance alternative measures (must conserve capital for payouts). Uninsured depositors (esp. corporates) gain better ranking → may shift from bond-buying to deposits.

Foundational model of bank fragility. Demand deposits offer liquidity insurance to consumers with uncertain cash needs. Two equilibria: good (only early types withdraw) and bad (run = self-fulfilling panic). Nobel Prize 2022.

1. Deposit insurance (eliminates run incentive). 2. Lender of Last Resort (Bagehot's rule). 3. Suspension of convertibility (closes the bank to new withdrawals). Each addresses the coordination failure differently.

Non-monetary effects of the financial crisis in the propagation of the Great Depression. Bank failures impair credit intermediation → real-economy effects beyond the monetary channel. Nobel Prize 2022.

MM says capital structure doesn't matter in a frictionless world. Fails for banks because: (1) deposit insurance creates a subsidy, (2) information asymmetry, (3) tax deductibility of interest, (4) regulatory constraints.

front: BRRD — Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive
back: EU framework (2014/59/EU) for managing bank failures without taxpayer bail-out. Three phases: normal → recovery (bank-led) → resolution (authority-led). Four resolution tools.

Recovery plan: written by the BANK; measures the bank can take itself to restore health (capital raise, dividend suspension, asset sales). Resolution plan: written by AUTHORITIES; how they would handle failure.

front: FOLF — Failing Or Likely to Fail (four triggers)
back: 1. No longer meets authorisation requirements. 2. Liabilities > assets. 3. Cannot pay debts as they fall due. 4. Requires extraordinary public support.
1. Bail-in. 2. Sale of business. 3. Bridge institution. 4. Asset separation (bad bank). Authority chooses the tool(s) based on circumstances.
Recapitalise the bank by writing down equity and converting subordinated debt and senior non-preferred bonds to new equity. NO taxpayer money. Removes the implicit too-big-to-fail subsidy.
Recapitalise the bank with EXTERNAL public funds (taxpayer-financed). Used widely in 2008–09 (RBS, Citi, AIG). The pre-2008 default; post-2008 reforms make bail-in the new default.

Large systemic banks expected to be bailed out by governments rather than allowed to fail. Markets price in the implicit guarantee → cheaper funding → unfair subsidy → incentivises further size and risk.
(1) No taxpayer money — losses absorbed inside the bank. (2) Markets price bail-in risk → implicit subsidy disappears. (3) Creditors and management have skin in the game. Requires credible MREL.
Bottom-up loss absorption: 1. Equity → 2. AT1 hybrid → 3. T2 subordinated → 4. Senior non-preferred → 5. Senior unsecured → 6. Deposits (uninsured first, then insured/covered).
1. Covered deposits (super-preference). 2. Retail/SME deposits not covered. 3. Senior bonds. 4. Non-preferred bonds. 5. T2 subordinated. 6. AT1 hybrid. Equity below all.
Bond category created post-BRRD. Explicitly subordinated to senior unsecured for resolution but ranks above subordinated debt. Designed to be bail-in-able and to count toward MREL.
Lilledal Savingsbank: target CET1 12% × REA 700 = 84 needed. Sources: 20 (old equity) + 10 (AT1) + 20 (T2) + 34 (non-preferred senior) = 84 ✓. Senior unsecured + deposits untouched.

Environmental (climate, resources, pollution), Social (labour, community, consumer protection), Governance (board, compensation, corruption, risk culture). Transversal driver of credit/market/operational/reputational risk.

Acute: extreme weather (floods, hurricanes, wildfires) → direct losses on collateral and borrowers. Chronic: long-term shifts (sea level, drought) → declining property values, rising NPLs in vulnerable regions.

Risk from shifting to a low-carbon economy. (1) Regulatory: carbon prices, emissions caps, disclosure mandates. (2) Market: stranded assets, divestment. (3) Reputational: brand damage, activist pressure.

front: TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures
back: Voluntary framework (now mandatory in many jurisdictions) for reporting climate risk: governance, strategy, risk management, metrics & targets. Foundation for CSRD-style mandatory disclosure.
EU mandatory sustainability reporting framework. Requires double-materiality assessment (impact ON and FROM the firm). Credible transition plans mandatory if material risks identified.
(1) Financial materiality: how sustainability factors affect the firm's financial performance. (2) Impact materiality: how the firm affects society and environment. EU CSRD requires both.

front: EBA Guidelines on ESG Risk Management (2024)
back: Banks must integrate ESG into governance, risk appetite, internal controls, risk assessment, management, and reporting. Capital add-ons possible if ESG-risk management is insufficient under CRD VI.

Net-zero financed/investment emissions by 2050. By 2030: oil & gas −25% intensity, shipping −33%, commercial property −25–35%. NOK 1500bn to sustainable transition by 2030. NOK 100bn assets in sustainable funds by 2025.

Sale of a security with simultaneous agreement to buy back at a higher price on a future date. Economically a secured loan. Primary funding tool of shadow banking. Central to 2007–09 crisis ("run on repo").
Discount applied to the market value of collateral. A 10% haircut on a €100 bond means borrower receives only €90. Higher haircuts = less leverage achievable + protect lender against price moves.
2007–09: haircuts on structured-product collateral spiked from ~0% to ~50%. Equivalent to a bank run on shadow-banking funding. Forced fire sales, debt cascades, liquidity spirals.
Short-term unsecured promissory notes issued by corporates and FIs. Maturities typically a few weeks to a few months (≤270 days for ABCP). Frozen during 2007–08, prompting Fed AMLF facility.
Unsecured short-term loans between banks. Reference rates: NIBOR (Norway), EURIBOR (EU), SOFR (US, secured replacement for LIBOR). Froze August 2007 → marked start of GFC interbank stress.

front: Repo vs CP vs interbank lending
back: Repo: SECURED, very short-term. Commercial paper: UNSECURED, weeks to months. Interbank: UNSECURED, often overnight. Repo borrower bears haircut; CP/interbank lender bears full credit exposure.
Higher haircuts mean less can be borrowed against the same collateral → forced selling to raise cash → collateral prices fall → haircuts widen further → procyclical death spiral.
FVtPL: mark-to-market, P&L impact immediate. AFS: fair value through OCI. HTM: amortised cost; fair value DISCLOSED only. SVB lesson: HTM hid $15.9bn losses while capital ratios looked adequate.

Bond portfolio classification has REAL crisis consequences. Held-to-Maturity classification let SVB avoid recognising mark-to-market losses on long Treasuries — but the economic insolvency was real and the run forced the losses to be realised.

When a bank makes a loan, it CREATES a matching deposit. Loans create deposits, not the other way around (BoE 2014 Quarterly Bulletin). Reserves are not the binding constraint in modern fiat systems — capital and demand are.

Norges Bank's swap arrangement: banks swapped illiquid covered bonds and mortgages for government T-bills. Restored interbank trust without recapitalisation. Norway avoided solvency crisis (it was a liquidity crisis there).
A: 75–100. B: 65–74. C: 55–64. D: 45–54. E: 35–44. F: 0–34. Same scale on May 2025 final and Spring 2024 final. Partial credit available on all questions.

6 questions, 100 points, 3-hour digital school exam. Mix: T/F-with-explanation (15–25 pts), conceptual essays (15–25 pts), numerical problems (15–25 pts: IFRS 9 impairment, capital ratios, FX swap pricing, bail-in calc).
